text.content: The internal operations agent they had built was holding up well. It handled inventory status queries, flagged supplier delays, and summarised fulfilment backlogs without breaking a sweat. So when the client support team asked whether the same architecture could be extended to handle inbound client queries, the answer had seemed obvious: just give it more instructions.

text.content: Six weeks later, the extended agent was struggling. It mixed up commercial queries with technical ones, gave billing answers to integration questions, and occasionally surfaced supplier data in responses to clients asking about API rate limits. The agent was not broken. It was overloaded. Vela's team had hit one of the most common and least-obvious ceilings in agent design: the point where a single agent's responsibilities become too broad for it to stay coherent.

text.content: Every time a user sends a message, the agent's LLM (the model behind the node) reads three things together: the system prompt (its instructions and persona), the conversation history (what has been said so far), and the user's current message. From those three inputs it decides what to do: call a tool, ask a clarifying question, or generate a response directly.

text.content: This means a single agent's coherence depends entirely on its ability to hold a clear, consistent mental model of its purpose across every possible input it might receive. When the range of inputs is narrow and well-defined, that works well. When the range becomes wide, the agent's instructions grow longer, its context window fills faster, and its responses become less consistent at the edges.

text.content: If you run a test set across an agent and notice that it handles one category of query reliably but another category poorly, the issue is usually not the instructions. It is that the agent is being asked to apply different levels of specialisation simultaneously, and the LLM context that makes it good at one category competes with the context that would make it good at the other. Vela's team found their agent scored well on fulfilment queries and poorly on commercial queries in the same session. The fix was separation.

text.content: This is the most dangerous signal because it is the hardest to catch in testing. When a single agent handles everything, there is no routing failure. Every query lands with the same agent, so there are no visible handoff errors. But the agent may answer a technical query with commercial language, or vice versa, in a way that sounds confident and coherent but is subtly wrong. This is the failure mode that only shows up when a subject-matter expert reviews the output.

text.content: The diagnosis is overload, not under-specification. The agent handling fulfilment queries works well with a single agent because its responsibilities are narrow and consistent. The client support use case, by contrast, spans two distinct domains with different knowledge bases, different tones, and different downstream actions. That is the kind of breadth that earns a multi-agent design.

text.content: Summary

rich_text.plain_text: Summary

text.content: The Vela team's instinct to extend their internal operations agent to cover client support was reasonable. What they discovered is that the breadth of the client support use case (commercial queries, technical queries, and hybrid queries that touch both) made a single agent inconsistent in ways that better instructions could not fix. That is overload, and it is the specific condition that a multi-agent design resolves.

text.content: The three signals (a system prompt trying to be two experts, quality that varies by query type, and plausible-but-wrong responses at the boundaries) give you a diagnostic framework you can apply to any agent before deciding whether to split it. The key discipline is checking for underspecification first. A poorly specified agent will still be poorly specified after you add a second one.
